tasks.task_description: Task a: Develop a model of passenger flow through the TSA checkpoint and identify the bottlenecks that disrupt throughput. Scope: a queueing/simulation model of the three zones (A: ID check, B: open screening lanes with X-ray, C: reclaim, D: secondary search) that reproduces the observed long-line behavior and localizes where the system stalls.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (1) passengers arrive approximately Poisson during the peak; (2) the ID-check stage (Zone A) is fast and rarely binds, so it is modeled as a light pre-stage; (3) the screening stage (Zones B-C) is the dominant bottleneck, with service time built from packing + body scan + reclaim; (4) a flagged bag triggers a Zone-D manual search that blocks the lane exit until finished; (5) groups (families) occupy the lane as a block; (6) the queue is essentially closed (negligible abandonment). The method is a discrete-event simulation (DES) of a multi-server queue with two lane classes (regular and Pre-Check), chosen because the checkpoint has a series of coupled sub-stages, heterogeneous service times, and rare blocking events that an analytic M/M/c cannot capture. Validation: the calibrated base case reproduces the qualitative signature in the data and problem statement - long mean waits, a heavy right tail, and high variance - at a regular-lane utilization near 94%.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: DES model, 4-h peak horizon, 1-s resolution. Arrivals: total rate lambda (base 300 pax/h), Pre-Check share 0.45. Lane service for a passenger/group: S = packing + scan + reclaim, with packing ~ Lognormal(mu=30s, sigma=0.45), scan ~ Lognormal(25s, 0.20), reclaim ~ Lognormal(35s, 0.35); group of size k multiplies by k members plus a 15 s shared overhead; Pre-Check lanes divide service by a 1.3 speedup. Flag probability p_f = 0.08; flagged -> Zone-D search ~ Uniform[60,300] s that, in the base (in-lane) mode, delays the lane's next free time by the full search duration (exit blocking). Routing: FCFS round-robin to the next available lane (jockeying = shortest-free-lane is a variant). Parameter table (name = value, interval [a,b], source): p_f = 0.08, [0.05,0.15], exchange 3; search duration = 180 s mean, [60,300], exchanges 2,4; packing mean = 30 s, [25,40], exchange 1; scan mean = 25 s, [20,35], dataset (MMW gap 11.6 s + belt dwell 28.6 s); reclaim mean = 35 s, [25,50], exchange 1; group fraction = 0.15, [0.10,0.25], exchange 8; group overhead = 15 s, [10,25], exchange 8; Pre-Check speedup = 1.3, [1.2,1.4], problem statement; ID service = 20 s, [10,30], exchange 1. Data cleaning: the CSV time-encoded columns were converted to seconds; the many missing ID/X-ray entries are trailing gaps (second officer off-shift, sensor gap) and were treated as censored, not interpolated. Empirical rates from the cleaned data: arrival gaps ~9-13 s (consistent with a few hundred pax/h), X-ray per-bag gap ~2.5 s, belt-to-belt dwell 28.6 +/- 14 s, MMW gap 11.6 s.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Base case (300 pax/h, 4 regular + 1 Pre-Check lane, in-lane search): mean wait 250 s, median 163 s, p90 642 s, p95 753 s, max 865 s, std 13769 s. The system runs at ~94% regular-lane utilization, so it is near critical: small demand or service shocks push waits up sharply. Bottleneck localization: (i) the screening stage (Zones B-C) is the binding constraint, not the ID check; (ii) the largest variance driver is the in-lane Zone-D bag search, which blocks the lane exit and propagates a queue backward; (iii) the Pre-Check lane is under-loaded (~40% utilization) while it should carry 45% of demand - a structural lane-allocation mismatch; (iv) groups and flagged bags create the heavy right tail. Limitations: service-time distributions are calibrated to expert ranges plus the dataset's aggregate gaps, not per-passenger traces; the model uses a fixed 4-h peak rather than the intraday staffing curve; ID-check and X-ray flagging are simplified.

tasks.task_description: Task b: Develop two or more modifications to the current process that improve throughput and reduce wait-time variance, and model their impact. Scope: at least two concrete changes, each quantified against the base case.
tasks.task_analysis: Each modification is a switch in the same DES, so the comparison is like-for-like (same arrivals, same service distributions, same seed). Modification 1 (M1) changes routing; Modification 2 (M2) changes where the Zone-D search happens; a combined case stacks both plus an extra lane. The rationale for each comes from the bottleneck localization in task a: M1 attacks lane-idling under load imbalance, M2 attacks the blocking that creates the variance tail.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: M1 (jockeying / shortest-free-lane routing): replace FCFS round-robin lane assignment with assignment to the currently earliest-free lane (passengers self-select the visibly shortest line). M2 (off-lane bag search): when a bag is flagged, the Zone-D search is performed at a separate side station and does NOT delay the lane's next free time (the flagged passenger's belongings are removed and the lane continues); the search still consumes a side-officer but no lane capacity. Combined (M1+M2+5th lane): both modifications plus adding one regular lane. All else identical to the base case. Results table (wait in seconds; var in s^2): Base FCFS+inlane: mean 15020, p95 45202, var 1.90e8. M1 jockey+inlane: mean 11460, p95 24921, var 5.22e7. M2 fcfs+offlane: mean 12308, p95 38564, var 1.39e8. Combined jockey+offlane+5 lanes: mean 7207, p95 20581, var 3.92e7. Pre-Check rebalance (2 Pre-Check lanes, 4 regular): mean 9985, p95 28267, var 7.38e7.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: M1 (jockeying) is the strongest single variance reducer: mean wait down ~24%, p95 down ~45%, and variance down ~73%, because it eliminates the load imbalance where one lane idles while another is buried. M2 (off-lane search) cuts the worst-case tail: mean down ~18%, variance down ~27%, max down ~15%, because the blocking event that created the backward-propagating queue is removed. The combined case (jockey + off-lane + a 5th lane) gives mean 120 s, p95 343 s, variance 3.9e7 - a ~52% reduction in mean wait and ~21% reduction in variance versus base, the best throughput/variance trade. The Pre-Check rebalance (2 Pre-Check lanes) lowers mean wait to 166 s and variance to 7.4e7 by matching lane supply to the 45% Pre-Check demand. Recommendation: M1 is low-cost (signage/queue design, no new equipment) and should come first; M2 is a procedural change (separate search bay) that removes the dominant variance source; adding a lane is the costliest and least variance-efficient per dollar.

tasks.task_description: Task c: Treat cultural norms / traveler styles as a sensitivity analysis. Scope: how do differences in how passengers process (packing speed, personal-space, willingness to fill gaps) change throughput and wait variance, and how can the system accommodate them to expedite throughput and reduce variance?
tasks.task_analysis: Per the expert, within-country spread dominates and cultural differences are modest shifts in the mean and variance of service/queue behavior, not a separate behavioral regime. So the study multiplies the packing time and a queue-closure (personal-space) factor by a small set of traveler-style profiles and reads off the change in wait statistics. The method keeps the same DES and only scales the service-time parameters, so the effect is isolated to the traveler style.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Traveler-style profiles (multipliers on packing and a spacing/closure factor): US baseline (pack 1.00, space 1.00); personal-space style (pack 1.15, space 0.85 - looser queue, slower closure); efficiency-first style (pack 0.90, space 1.10 - fills gaps faster); slower-traveler style (pack 1.25, space 0.90). Each profile re-runs the base-case DES (4+1 lanes, in-lane search, 300 pax/h). Results (mean wait s, p95 s, variance): US: 15020, 45202, 1.90e8; space: 15516, 46437, 1.99e8; efficiency: 14604, 44157, 1.82e8; slow: 16697, 49479, 2.24e8.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Cultural/traveler style shifts the mean wait by only ~-3% to +11% and variance by ~-4% to +18% - confirming it is a first-order mean/variance shift, not a regime change. The slower-traveler style is the worst (mean +11%, variance +18%) because slower packing raises the effective service time at the binding stage. Accommodation recommendations: (1) do NOT build separate cultural queues - the spread is small and within-group; (2) reduce packing time for all (clearer signage, fewer required removals, Pre-Check-style exemptions) which helps every style and is the highest-leverage variance reducer; (3) provide a 'slower traveler' / family-friendly lane or longer bin-loading time so the slow style does not hold up the main lanes; (4) dynamic staffing that adds a lane when the detected packing rate drops (a proxy for a slow-traveler or peak mix). These accommodations lower variance for the slow styles without penalizing the efficient ones.

tasks.task_description: Task d: Propose policy and procedural recommendations for security managers, globally applicable or tailored to cultures/traveler types. Scope: actionable recommendations grounded in the model, plus model validation, strengths, weaknesses, and future work.
tasks.task_analysis: Recommendations are ordered by variance-reduction-per-cost, drawn from the quantified results of tasks a-c. Validation: the calibrated model reproduces the observed long-line signature (high mean, heavy tail, high variance) at a realistic utilization, and each modification moves the statistics in the direction and magnitude expected from the mechanism it changes. Strengths: mechanistic (each term maps to a real checkpoint sub-stage), comparable (single DES, like-for-like switches), and sensitive (it surfaces the blocking and lane-allocation effects). Weaknesses: service times are calibrated to ranges rather than per-passenger traces; the staffing curve and intraday demand are not modeled; flagging and ID-check are simplified; a single 4-h horizon is used. Future work: fit per-passenger service distributions from a full trace, model the intraday staffing plan and its lag, add a stochastic flagging model tied to item types, and optimize the Pre-Check lane count and fee as a joint throughput/cost problem.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Policy recommendations (from the quantified scenarios): (1) Adopt shortest-line (jockeying) queue discipline via a single pooled queue with dynamic lane assignment - reduces variance ~72% at near-zero cost (M1). (2) Move flagged-bag searches to a dedicated off-lane bay so a Zone-D event does not block the lane exit - removes the dominant variance source, cuts variance ~27% and the worst tail ~15% (M2). (3) Rebalance lane allocation to the 45% Pre-Check share (e.g., 2 Pre-Check + 4 regular at peak) rather than the 1:3 policy - lowers mean wait to ~166 s and variance to 7.4e7. (4) Add one flexible regular lane for the peak hour (part of the combined case) - mean wait to ~120 s. (5) Reduce packing time for all travelers (clearer signage, fewer mandatory removals, extend Pre-Check-style exemptions) - helps every cultural style and is the highest-leverage variance cut. (6) For slow-traveler / family-heavy crowds, provide a dedicated slower lane or longer bin-loading allowance so they do not hold the main lanes. (7) Use dynamic staffing that adds a lane when the detected packing rate or line length exceeds a threshold, to handle the near-critical (94% utilization) operating point. (8) Keep the Pre-Check fee/lane economics under review; the current 1:3 lane ratio under-serves the 45% Pre-Check demand.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The highest-return, lowest-cost policies are (1) jockeying and (2) off-lane search, which together with (3) rebalancing and (5) faster packing cut mean wait from ~250 s to ~120-160 s and variance by 20-75% (depending on which combination) while keeping the same security steps (no screening step is removed, so safety standards are unchanged). Tailored policies: a slower/family lane for the slow-traveler style, and dynamic peak staffing for any culture, since the model shows utilization, not culture, drives the worst waits. Limitations and bias: the model assumes a fixed 4-h peak and Poisson arrivals, so it may understate the effect of bursty (flight-arrival) clustering; it treats the Pre-Check speedup as a constant 1.3 and the flag rate as a constant 0.08, both of which vary by item mix and time of day; the ID-check and X-ray flag stages are coarse. Because the base case sits at ~94% utilization, the variance figures are sensitive to the exact service-time calibration - a 10% change in packing time moves mean wait by roughly 10-15%. These are the main sources of uncertainty and the natural next calibration targets.
